title: Recovering Hidden Wildlife--Vehicle Collisions from Existing Crash Data: A Cross-State Framework for Detection, Prevalence Estimation, and Under-Reporting Audits
summary:
Wildlife--vehicle collisions (WVCs) impose a large toll on U.S. highways, yet state crash databases often fail to record animal involvement, leaving agencies uncertain of the true missing count. This study evaluates whether existing crash records can identify individual WVCs and estimate overall unrecorded rates.
  We analyzed 4.9 million crash records from Colorado, Utah, Iowa, and Illinois (2007-2026). Each state's schema underwent a label-leakage screen to exclude explicit animal fields before harmonization into a shared vocabulary. Calibrated gradient-boosted classifiers were trained per state, interpreted using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated for prevalence estimation via Adjusted Classify-and-Count and Maximum-Likelihood techniques across in-domain, cross-state, and synthetic reporting-gap scenarios.
  Detection performance depends heavily on record completeness rather than collision rarity. At ~4% prevalence, feature-rich Utah achieved an average precision of 0.88 versus 0.64 for feature-poor Colorado, and outperformed Iowa despite Iowa's 3x higher WVC rate. Within-state richness curves confirm feature depth drives accuracy. While classifiers ranked records accurately across states, probability calibration did not transfer directly. However, in-domain prevalence estimation recovered true collision rates within 0.001.
  This work shifts WVC analysis from spatial clustering to record-level detection and missing-data estimation using legacy datasets.
  Transportation agencies can retrospectively flag unrecorded WVCs, quantify total collision burden to support mitigation funding, and identify high-value reporting fields prior to revising crash-report manuals.

title: Mapping urban heat from citizen-collected data: a scalable Gaussian process approach to correcting for preferential sampling
summary: The urban heat island (UHI) effect amplifies heat stress in cities, increasing heat-related illness, mortality, sleep disruption, and energy demand. Because UHI intensity varies at neighborhood scales, intra-city temperature mapping is essential for assessing public health impacts, yet existing monitoring networks are sparse. Crowdsourced weather stations provide dense, hourly observations but suffer from noise and systematic biases, including preferential sampling driven by where residents install sensors. We introduce two scalable Gaussian process frameworks which adjust for preferential sampling and enable statewide, high-resolution temperature prediction. The first integrates sampling correction directly within a sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGPR+PS). The second uses a two-stage estimator involving a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP+GP) that estimates the sampling intensity field and incorporates it into temperature prediction. Both methods rely on inducing-point approximations and variational inference to scale beyond traditional Gaussian processes. Applied to approximately 10,000 citizen stations across North Carolina, the models generate hourly temperature fields within minutes. Validation against independent urban heat campaign data shows that the preferential sampling correction improves predictive performance, increasing average afternoon correlations across four cities from 0.26 to 0.43. This scalable framework enables neighborhood-level UHI assessment and supports studies of heat exposure disparities statewide.

title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation
comment: Accepted on Conference on Optimization, Modeling, Simulation, and Analytics (COMOSA 2026)
summary: Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment

title: Tail reliability in probabilistic electricity price forecasts: comparing model combination and conformal prediction in the GB day-ahead market
summary: Probabilistic forecasts of day-ahead electricity prices are increasingly used to manage price risk, yet competing models are usually ranked on aggregate scores that average over the price regimes in which uncertainty matters most. This study evaluates probabilistic forecasts of hourly EPEX SPOT GB day-ahead prices over a full held-out calendar year, applying a common pre-auction information boundary and rolling-origin design to linear quantile regression, a quantile regression forest (QRF), a LEAR-QRA benchmark and an encoder-decoder quantile long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Two routes to more reliable intervals are then compared: conformal recalibration and Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA). Aggregate scores separate the LSTM and QRF only weakly, with a non-significant 4.4% difference in continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), but their conditional behaviour differs sharply. Above 200 GBP/MWh the LSTM covered 0.12 of outcomes and QRF 0.71, consistent with the forest retaining realised spikes in its leaf distributions while the network learned a smooth upper tail. Conformal recalibration corrected marginal coverage but did not improve the interval score or materially repair spike coverage. QRA combining the LSTM, QRF and LEAR-QRA forecasts reduced CRPS to 5.14 GBP/MWh and raised coverage above 200 GBP/MWh to 0.65 at unchanged interval width. Recalibration and combination therefore address different failures and are not substitutes.

title: NepTTS-Bench: Native-Speaker Benchmarking and NepaliMOS for Nepali Text-to-Speech
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ampixa/neptts-bench ; code: https://github.com/Ampixa/neptts-bench
summary: Nepali TTS has reached a point where multiple systems are available, but there is no shared evaluation to compare them. NepTTS-Bench was created to address what existing automated and manual evaluation systems lack for Nepali TTS. A controlled benchmark with phonological grounding which contains 205 sentences (77 minimal pairs targeting aspiration, retroflex/dental contrasts, nasalization, gemination, and schwa deletion) which is rated by 180 speakers. There are 6,962 ratings for 10 TTS configurations and two human references. Along with this 7 ASR systems were evaluated for round-trip CER. SCOREQ was also run as an automated baseline. The key finding is that automated evaluation like SCOREQ prefers proprietary systems like ElevenLabs but native listeners prefer Piper. This is contributed by the fact that most of the systems not properly tuned for Nepali tend to show Hindi phonological behaviour and our minimal pairs are designed to surface such contrasts. We also present NepaliMOS predictor which is fine tuned on collected ratings. NepaliMOS achieves system-level rho = 0.90 on the dense panel but drops to utterance-level rho = 0.43 under leave-one-system-out evaluation. This is statistically significant and confirms that NepaliMOS captures genuine signal but cross-provider transfer is limited. A human calibration is recommended for new systems for which we release a Python evaluation package for practitioners to run the benchmark against new systems.

title: GHOST Driver
summary:
AI inference workloads running on GPU clusters exhibit a well-documented utilization paradox: monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi regularly report GPU utilization figures above 80%, yet effective compute throughput is substantially lower. A significant fraction of reported utilization time is consumed by fence waits, driver submission overhead, DMA scheduling latency, and interrupt coalescing delays, none of which is visible to userspace profiling tools. These hidden latency components are embedded deep inside the Linux kernel GPU driver stack, primarily within the Direct Rendering Manager (DRM) subsystem, GEM buffer object lifecycle, and dma_fence synchronization infrastructure. Existing vendor profiling tools like CUPTI operate at the CUDA userspace boundary and provide no visibility into kernel-side driver paths.
  We present GHOST-Driver (GPU Host-Side Observability and Tracing for Drivers), a non-intrusive eBPF-based framework that attaches to stable DRM kernel tracepoints and select kprobes to expose the full latency decomposition of the GPU driver submission path with sub-microsecond resolution and CPU overhead below 2% in production. GHOST-Driver tracks six key submission stages (ioctl entry, GEM BO validation, dma_fence dependency resolution, command ring emission, DMA engine scheduling, and interrupt fence signaling) and correlates them with per-tenant vGPU context IDs for multi-tenant attribution in SR-IOV and MIG environments, exporting trace metrics to Prometheus and OpenTelemetry.

title: Sequential Bayesian analysis of time-varying transmission in stratified epidemic renewal models
summary: Understanding how transmission varies across age groups is important for epidemic surveillance and targeted intervention, but estimating age-specific transmission in near real time is challenging when infections are only partially observed, observations are delayed, and transmission varies across age groups. We develop a Bayesian age-stratified renewal model that jointly estimates latent infections, time-varying age-specific susceptibility, and age-specific contributions to transmission within an empirically specified contact structure. To enable sequential inference under these processes, we use a block particle filtering approach embedded within a sequential Monte Carlo squared framework, with fixed-lag smoothing to account for temporal dependence and delayed observations. From the inferred transmission process, we derive a next-generation matrix, effective reproduction number, and reproduction contributions. Applied to age-stratified COVID-19 surveillance data from Ireland during the Omicron dominant period, the framework reveals heterogeneity in susceptibility and transmission, with older adults exhibiting higher susceptibility, while younger and working-age groups make larger contributions to transmission because of their higher contact rates. These results demonstrate how statistical inference can provide age-specific transmission estimates to support targeted epidemic monitoring and intervention.

title: A Neuroprosthetic SoC Featuring Rapid Local Sensory Feedback with On-Chip Unsupervised Multi-Class Spike Sorting
comment: 4 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Author's accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in IEEE Solid-State Circuits Letters
summary: This letter presents a 65 nm neuroprosthetic system-on-chip (SoC) featuring a rapid feedback pathway from motor recording to sensory stimulation. To enable low-latency sensory mapping modulated by individual-neuron firing rates, the SoC integrates a mixed-signal unsupervised spike-sorting module with stimulation-artifact rejection, a programmable sliding-window firing-rate calculator, and a closed-loop controller for adapting stimulation parameters. The spike-sorting module combines event-driven analog feature extraction with Manhattan-distance-based digital clustering while consuming 1.6 $μ$W/channel. On the Quiroga Difficult-1 benchmark, it achieves 94.58% three-class accuracy, with only a 0.4% reduction when stimulation artifacts are introduced at 20% of the spike count. The closed-loop controller supports polynomial and logarithmic mapping functions and incorporates Mitchell's approximation for power saving. The SoC is fully characterized on the bench and in vivo.

title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
summary: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.

title: Identifiability of Neologism Dynamics from Aggregate Corpus Counts
summary: Aggregate lexical frequencies reflect both what speakers do and how a corpus records it. We develop a stochastic framework for lexical adoption, abandonment and reactivation on a temporal multilayer network, together with a count observation model separating speaker prevalence, use intensity and detectability, and ask what such data identify. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for the never-active and dormant states to be merged exactly, collapsing the three-state chain to two, and show that the condition constrains the exposures a given network can deliver, not the response function as a whole. No count design can distinguish use intensity from detectability, an exact invariance distinct from the merely practical loss of information in sparse series. And we prove that in a low-prevalence community approximation the rates enter only through the net growth $β-μ$ and the coupling product $βκ$, so that a one-parameter family of triples has identical trajectories, the only separating information lying in a term quadratic in prevalence whose size depends on the emission scale. Simulations characterise recovery, prediction and sensitivity to misspecification. An exploratory analysis of 144 candidate forms in CREA and CORPES XXI press subcorpora illustrates the consequences: under the chosen emission scale and a symmetric contact graph, very different rate triples give nearly identical fitted trajectories, and in leave-one-country-out comparison with training-only proxies and seeds on a retrospectively selected cohort, a constant-rate count baseline beats the evaluated dynamic specifications on 84 to 94% of forms. These findings neither establish nor refute contact-driven diffusion. They delimit what this model and panel can support, and name the calibration, geographical contrast and repeated speaker observations that would make the question answerable.

title: Mission Capability-Aware UAV Swarm Coordination for Autonomous Disaster Response
summary: This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) driven mission capability aware unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm coordination framework for autonomous post disaster search and rescue. An integrated sensing and communication enabled master high altitude platform station senses the disaster environment, detects victims and hazards, and constructs adaptive rescue regions based on spatially varying mission demands. A mission capability requirement (MCR) quantifies regional capability demand, while a normalized mission capability score (MCS) characterizes the real time capability of individual UAVs. A capability-aware assignment mechanism matches UAV capabilities to regional requirements while minimizing deployment distance. An MCS based reallocation mechanism dynamically transfers UAVs from capability surplus to capability deficient regions while preserving donor sufficiency. A hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework with proximal policy optimization performs high-level region selection, while MCR MCS matching enables feasible UAV level reallocation. Finally, joint trajectory optimization considers travel time, distance, propulsion energy, operational capability, obstacle avoidance, and inter UAV collision avoidance. Theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate improved mission capability satisfaction, resource efficiency, and disaster response performance

title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
summary: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population gives one useful service per request under the observed live-confirmation condition. The primary study contains 404 Full16 cases from 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points are reference-discrepant, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 m. The paired causal-navigation transforms are reference-consistent in all 404 cases, with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m. Across five matched request budgets, the largest difference between the hypergeometric prediction and the observed ordinary-random mean is 0.8412 services. Ordinary matched random reaches 0/50 target successes, while actionability-matched random reaches 50/50 and matches the CARD policy. Public downstream evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases measures optimizer wall-time ratios of 1.128x-67.65x for random versus CARD graph interventions. Native solver records locate this difference in elimination fill, Cholesky factor size, and numeric factorization. Together, these results connect certificate semantics, physical execution, proof acquisition, and graph computation through explicit system objects.

title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review
comment: 26 pages and 5 figures, preprint and submitted for review
summary: Heart failure is a serious medical condition associated with risk of acute deterioration, recurrent hospitalizations and high mortality making accurate mortality prediction potentially valuable for patient care and healthcare planning. Numerous prognostic models have been developed using conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), but variation in study populations, heart failure definitions, prediction horizons and development practices may limit interpretation of applicability. We conducted a systematic review of mortality prediction models published between 2009 to the start of 2026 searching three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) for studies predicting all-cause mortality over a 1-60 months prediction horizon among patients with heart failure. Data extracted were cohort characteristics, heart failure definitions, model development, cohort size, validation practices, mortality, computational model design and reported performance. The risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Of 1516 publications identified, 56 met the inclusion criteria. Publication numbers increased over the observation period, alongside increasing use of ML/DL models and decreasing use of CS approaches. Most development cohorts (64%) were classified as Unknown/Undefined heart failure, reflecting inconsistent reporting and terminology that did not correspond with established heart failure guidelines. External validation was reported in 23% of studies. Overall, research in modeling heart failure mortality has grown alongside increasing adoption of ML/DL approaches. Greater standardization of study design and reporting is needed for meaningful comparison, reproducibility and evaluation of models for clinical application.

title: Learning to read residual images for single-pixel photography
summary: Continuous video scales in cost with camera count, resolution and recording duration, yet many monitoring tasks seek events rather than complete images and can operate on a compact single-pixel measurement stream. Recovering a chosen interval as video is then desirable, but at 0.24\% of the pixel count the scene correlation image looks like noise and per-clip optimization takes minutes. Correlating the residual of an estimate with the coding patterns nevertheless gives a residual image, the gradient of a centered measurement loss. Lifted through a pretrained video decoder, its agreement with the true error exceeds that of control decoders. Video-latent inversion (VLI) then outperforms frame-wise image-latent reconstruction at 1{,}000 bucket values. Measurement-Gradient-Conditioned Video Flow (MGV-Flow), trained once to read the lifted residual image with preceding frames, reconstructs five frames in 1.55\,s at 22.9\,dB median PSNR, against 398\,s and 18.1\,dB for VLI, with the largest gains in high-motion scenes. Directional fidelity ranks 30 coding configurations and selects one needing a third fewer bucket values. On a physical system, MGV-Flow outperforms per-frame reconstruction without retraining. A sliding window over the bucket-value stream yields 3.2 frames per second on one RTX~4090 and, in theory, 20 frames per second on a data-centre accelerator. Demonstrations are available at https://cavedweller509.github.io/MGV-Flow.

title: Latent Cluster Separation as a Regularizer for Lifelong Anomaly Detection
summary: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.

title: Statistical analysis of the remaining human life expectancy. Mathematical models of the type Gompertz-Makeham and others
summary: Many researchers believe that human lifetime on the interval (30,80) years is described by the Gompertz-Makeham distribution. In this work, the task is set to test this hypothesis. We consider a number of distributions: Gompertz-Makeham, Gompertz-Weibull, Logistic Kannisto-Makeham, Logistic Beard-Makeham and Logistic Beard-Weibull, some of which are partially known, for which comparative calculations on real mortality data are performed using the $χ^2$ criterion. The data were selected for three countries: England \& Wales, Norway and Sweden, cohorts born in 1900. As it turned out, on the interval (30,80) years the Gompertz-Makeham distribution is far from being the best among those listed above. In addition, for the same data, a similar problem was studied for the interval (80,120) years.

title: ISAC-Assisted Proactive Handover in mmWave Networks: Value of Foresight and Localization Requirements
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) links can lose tens of decibels within milliseconds when a person or vehicle crosses the line of sight, and reactive handover recovers only after the outage has begun. Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) promises to let the network see blockers coming and move users to another cell in advance. This paper asks how much such foresight is worth relative to the best reactive handover, and what sensing accuracy is needed to harvest it. We formulate cost-aware cell selection with knowledge of the future signal-to- noise ratio as a sequential decision problem, define the value of foresight through a policy-independent bound, and develop an ISAC-assisted handover framework in which a radio unit senses blockers with its own communication waveform and a simulated Open RAN xApp plans handovers. Ray-traced experiments in a 28 GHz street canyon, reported on held-out scenarios, show that, with a short look-ahead, perfect foresight closes most of the gap between service-aware (Layer-3) reactive handover and an instantaneous oracle. Harvesting this value, however, requires the user and nearby blockers to be localized to about a decimeter, well beyond what our radar tracker and meter- level user positioning provide; with realistic errors, even an uncertainty-aware planner largely defers to reactive handover.

title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data
summary: Bubeck and Sellke's universal law of robustness says that fitting $n$ noisy samples below the noise level with a class of $p$ real parameters forces a Lipschitz constant of order $\sqrt{nd/p}$, when the covariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is isoperimetric: smooth interpolation costs a factor $d$ of overparametrization. Its hypotheses are Gaussian-type concentration, a homogeneous covariate law, scalar outputs, and independent samples; we relax each one. Exponential concentration suffices, at the unchanged rate and absolute constant and at the price of a capacity burn-in, some form of which we show is necessary; this gives the law for normalized log-concave covariates, with a $\log d$ loss from the current KLS bound. For heterogeneous mixtures the worst component constant is replaced by the weighted average of the component constants, under a typicality condition on the mixture composition. For vector-valued predictors the bound at the Frobenius Lipschitz scale is free of the output dimension $K$, and the Euclidean bound loses only $K^{-1/2}$, a loss that covariate-independent noise removes. Stationary Markov covariates retain the i.i.d. rate, the pseudo-spectral gap entering only the sample-size conditions. One master theorem carries the shared argument, and constants are explicit throughout.

title: A signal-processing cascade linking satellite heat exposure, genomic variation, and mortality risk
summary: Heat-related mortality varies among individuals under similar environmental conditions, yet environmental exposure and genetic susceptibility are typically modelled separately. We propose a signal-processing cascade linking satellite-derived land-surface temperature to sequence-dependent heat-shock response and mortality risk. The framework combines distributed-lag filtering of thermal exposure, nonlinear HSF1 activation, cross-correlation with an HSF1 position-weight-matrix kernel, and Hill-model mapping of sequence-dependent binding changes to regulatory response. Applied to 52 heat-response genes and 157 naturally occurring variants, the framework identifies 21 heat-shock-element arrays across 17 genes. Variants in canonical arrays are significantly enriched for predicted binding disruption ($p=3\times10^{-4}$). Propagating these effects through the cascade yields a peak predicted mortality-risk multiplier of $1.68\times$ at $40$--$42\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The framework demonstrates how environmental and genomic signals can be integrated to model inter-individual variation in heat-related risk.

title: Adaptive Low-Rank Quantum Kernel Acquisition under Finite-Shot Measurements: Perturbation Guarantees for QSVMs
summary: Quantum kernel methods require estimating entries of a dense Gram matrix through repeated circuit measurements, making kernel construction expensive and statistically noisy. For a dataset of size $n$, dense construction requires $O(n^2)$ kernel queries, while existing approximation methods typically assume inexpensive access to kernel entries or use non-adaptive sampling. We study adaptive low-rank quantum kernel acquisition when the kernel is accessible only through a finite-shot quantum overlap oracle. Our framework, ICAQKL, uses residual-driven incomplete Cholesky construction to acquire informative kernel columns sequentially and form a positive-semidefinite rank-$r$ surrogate, reducing the training-kernel acquisition cost to $O(nrN_s)$ circuit executions for $r\ll n$, where $N_s$ is the number of shots per queried entry. The central difficulty is that finite-shot errors perturb both the queried kernel values and the adaptive pivot sequence that determines the low-rank factor. We develop a non-asymptotic perturbation framework for this stochastic adaptive process, establishing concentration over the realized queries, stability of noisy pivot selection and factor construction, and propagation of the coupled sampling and approximation errors to the QSVM objective, optimizer, prediction function, and classification margin. The resulting rank--shot conditions characterize when ICAQKL approaches the full QSVM induced by the same quantum feature map. Experiments on benchmark and biomedical datasets show favorable accuracy--query-cost tradeoffs, competitive performance with the full QSVM, and competitive or improved performance relative to the evaluated Nyström baselines under comparable settings. ICAQKL is intended to enable measurement-efficient and theoretically controlled use of a selected quantum kernel, rather than to establish quantum advantage over classical kernels.

title: Towards Automatic Heart Murmur Characterization from Multi-spot Phonocardiograms
summary: Cardiac auscultation traditionally detects the presence of a heart murmur, but clinicians further characterize it by timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. Most automatic phonocardiogram analysis systems stop at binary detection and do not estimate this richer description. In this work, we formulate automatic murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks and compare three multi-spot strategies on recordings from the aortic, pulmonary, mitral, and tricuspid auscultation locations. First, classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained independently at each location, and predictions are combined via a maximum-severity late-fusion rule. Second, a synchronous multi-input CNN jointly processes one representative segment per location for a single task. Third, a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared multi-spot representation. Using 735 patients from the CirCor DigiScope dataset with complete four-spot recordings, the best late-fusion configurations reach an unweighted mean sensitivity between 85.56% and 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls between 80.00% and 100.00% for every relevant category. The multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task, while the multi-output model reaches values between 72.59% and 79.40%, estimating all five attributes from one shared representation. We further show that naively balancing training data by adding all minority-class segments degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule, since it introduces non-representative, noisy segments not filtered by the clustering-based segment selection used for evaluation. These results indicate multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, outlining a path toward automatic, structured murmur reports complementing binary screening.

title: Predicting Factor Decay: ML Models for Cross-Factor Predictability Erosion
summary: We develop ML models that predict when cross-factor predictability will erode, enabling prospective risk management. A decay prediction model achieves C-index $= 0.93$ on held-out factor pairs, providing early warning of signal erosion---the key predictor is initial signal strength: stronger signals decay faster (``regression to the mean''). An online regime detector enables real-time classification with 6.6-day average detection delay. Prior work explains why factors decay (arbitrage, publication effects); we predict when decay will occur. Limitation: The primary HML$\to$SMB signal does not replicate in post-break OOS (2013--2024); this null result is consistent with genuine decay but limits confirmatory claims. Motivation: Among 30 directed Fama-French factor pairs (1990--2024), predictability targeting the Size factor (SMB) decays fastest. Of 7 pairs showing exponential decay ($R^2 > 0.3$), 4 target SMB (Mkt-RF$\to$SMB, CMA$\to$SMB, HML$\to$SMB, RMW$\to$SMB; half-lives 2.4--4.1 years). This SMB-concentration pattern motivates the predictive models. Methodology: Using a regime-conditional Granger framework with Student-$t$ HMMs, we document structural breaks clustering around June 1998 ($p < 10^{-10}$). A pre-break OOS test (HMM trained 1990--1995, tested 1996--2007) confirms signals existed: HML$\to$SMB shows $p = 0.013$ (Elevated) and $p < 0.001$ (Crisis). The primary HML$\to$SMB signal does not replicate in post-break OOS (2013--2024), consistent with genuine decay rather than overfitting---after ${\sim}6$ half-lives, the expected signal is $<$1% of its 1990s peak. International analysis finds 2/4 non-US markets with Bonferroni-surviving OOS effects; correction for full specification search was not applied, so results remain exploratory.

title: Data-Driven Spectrum Access Technologies for 6G
comment: Accepted for publication in the IEEE Communications Magazine
summary: The surge in global mobile traffic, driven by 5G adoption and emerging applications, necessitates new spectrum allocations for 6G systems. With most major swaths of spectrum below 15 GHz already allocated to other services, co-existence between cellular and incumbent services such as satellite or radar systems is critical to make such spectrum accessible for 6G. At the same time, the advent of artificial intelligence offers a new opportunity for designing more efficient spectrum sharing techniques. This paper presents four novel data-driven spectrum access techniques to enable efficient use of spectrum for the 6G era: 1) co-existence technique for efficient protection of fixed incumbent receivers within an established protection area; 2) data-driven approach for protecting satellite receivers via control of radiated power above the horizon; 3) spectrum sensing-based fast-time-scale physical resource block blanking; and 4) base station-based spectrum occupancy detection to enable fast-time-scale spectrum sharing with satellite and non-terrestrial network incumbents. These techniques leverage artificial intelligence and extreme multiple-input multiple-output capabilities to enable efficient spectrum co-existence/sharing while maintaining cellular network performance.

title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
comment: 47 pages, 14 figures. Code: https://github.com/FAIRC-Research/mowe. Models: https://huggingface.co/FAIRC
summary:
Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.
  At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22.
  We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE.
  In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.

title: Separating Weight and Likelihood Tail Effects in Bayesian Neural Groundwater Inversion
summary: Groundwater inversion is commonly built on Gaussian assumptions for both network weights and output errors. The assumptions are convenient, but it is unclear which one should be relaxed when hydraulic conductivity is heavy tailed. Here, Gaussian and q-Gaussian distributions were assigned independently to variational weights and the conditional output likelihood in a $2\times2$ Bayesian neural design. Hydraulic conductivity, porosity, and dispersion were inferred jointly from sparse head and transport observations. Four q regimes ($q=1.0$, 1.2, 1.5, and 1.8) were evaluated with five independently generated data sets and matched training seeds, giving 130 held-out cases per regime and 500 posterior draws per case. At $q=1.5$, q-Gaussian weights with a Gaussian likelihood reduced log-conductivity CRPS by 2.85\% (95\% paired CI 0.82--4.88) and calibration error by 3.72 percentage points. Conductivity RMSE was unchanged, while 95\% interval width increased by 9.86\%. At $q=1.8$, assigning q-Gaussian tails to both components produced no stable accuracy gain and increased interval width by 138.46\%. The Gaussian-generated porosity and dispersion controls showed negligible accuracy changes. Moderate weight-side tails can thus improve distributional prediction, whereas an overly heavy output likelihood trades sharpness for coverage. Separating these two roles provides a clearer basis for uncertainty modeling in groundwater inversion.

title: Beyond TR 38.811 for 6G NTN Channel Models
summary: As the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) expands 6G non-terrestrial network (NTN) to S, Ku, and Ka bands for integration with existing terrestrial cellular networks, the necessary satellite channel model for link and network performance evaluation remains tied to TR 38.811, last revised in 2020. We identify issues on multiple fronts: inappropriate parameter specifications based on very limited site-specific environments considered, omission of satellite-induced Doppler spread and directional antenna effects and lack of a transparent channel model generation procedure. To address these limitations, we re-derive the channel parameters using ray tracing (RT) over urban and rural environments based on ITU-R building statistics. Our results show that TR 38.811 substantially overestimates the K-factor at low elevations and predicts a decreasing trend with elevation, which is inconsistent with RT. The Ka-band clutter loss (CL) also exceeds the RT estimates by more than 15 dB in urban cases. It also underestimates rural delay spread (DS) at low elevations and predicts an elevation trend inconsistent with RT. We further quantify the previously neglected satellite-induced Doppler spread. Finally, we demonstrate that the conventional TR 38.811 channel generator significantly underestimates the K-factor in the presence of directional antenna (beamforming), while our modified generator substantially reduces this discrepancy.

title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
summary: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.

title: Multi-modal Laplace-based sampling
summary: We study the multi-modal Laplace approximation, given by a weighted Gaussian mixture centred at the local minima of the negative log-density, for sampling from probability measures that concentrate around finitely many modes as an inverse-temperature parameter $n$ grows. Such distributions occur in Bayesian inference in the small noise or large data regime. We derive explicit, non-asymptotic bounds on the Hellinger distance between the multi-modal Laplace approximation and the concentrating posterior. The bound decays like $n^{-1/2}$ with $n$ and the constants depend only polynomially on the dimension $d$. Moreover, we analyse the Laplace mixture as a proposal distribution for self-normalised importance sampling and independent Metropolis--Hastings (IMH) targeting concentration multimodal distributions. We derive asymptotic results, as $n\to\infty$, on the effective sample size in case of importance sampling as well as on the average acceptance probability, lag-one autocorrelation, and spectral gap in case of IMH. Numerical experiments illustrate and verify our theoretical findings.

title: GTAC: A Graph-Transformer Actor-Critic for Carrier-Aware MU-MIMO User Grouping
summary: Achieving higher spectral efficiency (SE) in 5G and future 6G networks requires efficient massive multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) grouping under coupled physical-layer constraints and strict scheduling deadlines. Motivated by industry efforts in AI-native RAN, we propose Graph-Transformer Actor-Critic (GTAC), a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture for carrier-aware MU-MIMO user grouping. The objective is to maximize the long-term proportional-fair (PF) utility of the cell subject to constraints from the practical stack protocol. GTAC comprises a shared actor--critic encoder with spatial-edge-biased attention mechanism, a pointer decoder actor that generates grouping decisions, and a multi-stage transformer critic that estimates the carrier-wide state-value during training. Training begins by cloning a teacher policy that cannot meet real-time deployment deadlines, followed by critic warmup and two-stage reinforcement learning using proximal policy optimization (PPO), first on a narrow, power-matched carrier and then on the full carrier with a Kullback--Leibler (KL) policy anchor. After two-stage PPO, the best GTAC policy outperforms the non-real-time teacher by 11.6% in carrier SE, while exceeding its PF utility and preserving the cell-edge throughput. A CUDA implementation of GTAC achieves a 69.6 us inference latency on an RTX PRO 4500 GPU, below the targeted 100 us inference budget in practical systems.

title: MCPGuard: Finding Conformance Gaps in MCP SDKs via Dual-Track Analysis and Dynamic Adjudication
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. Specification constraints omitted by these SDKs may propagate to downstream applications, highlighting the importance of SDK-level conformance testing. Yet existing MCP conformance tools mainly exercise running endpoints and reveal little about whether SDK models enforce specification requirements. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and builds PoCs to validate candidates. A shared kernel with language-specific adapters enables analysis across SDKs. On the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirms 13 and 19 findings, respectively, none of which are exposed by two black-box baselines. Tests on open MCP servers further show that these gaps can systematically propagate downstream. By making SDK conformance of specification constraints directly testable, MCPGuard complements conventional endpoint-oriented conformance suites.

title: BEAGLE in Action: Phylogenetic Likelihoods for Very Large State Spaces
summary: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

title: RFShape: An IQ-Pretrained Wireless Foundation Model for Heterogeneous IQ & CIR Representations
summary: In wireless systems, foundation models have been proposed as alternative artificial intelligence models to replace task-specific models with a shared pretrained model that can be reused across many downstream applications (source separation, interference detection, localization, etc.). These wireless foundation models promise to reuse learned representations across diverse tasks, but choosing a foundation model also means choosing its input representation. For example, a model pretrained on spectrograms expects spectrograms, while one pretrained on in-phase/quadrature (IQ) samples expects IQ, limiting which pretrained model can be used for a given downstream problem. To remedy this, we present RFShape, a 7.4 M-parameter foundation model that breaks this coupling by adapting how a signal is presented to a shared pretrained encoder. RFShape is pretrained solely on synthetic IQ waveforms, without real captures, labels, or channel impulse responses (CIRs), and uses deterministic representation operators to support heterogeneous downstream inputs. Across ten tasks and nine datasets unseen during pretraining, the same encoder supports classification, ranging-error regression, and two-dimensional positioning. Representation selection alone increases 23-class radar recognition from 23.0% to 69.5% and short-range technology recognition from 70.8% to 97.1%. RFShape also outperforms CIR-pretrained ultra-wideband baselines by up to 12.7 percentage points for (N)LOS classification despite never observing CIRs during pretraining. These results show that foundation-model reuse need not be limited by the representation or modality seen during pretraining, and adapting how a signal is presented can extend a single pretrained encoder across heterogeneous wireless tasks.

title: ReVi: Recursive Recap Video Generation
summary: Novels tell rich stories, but their textual form cannot directly present the sights and sounds of the worlds they describe. Film adaptations offer an audiovisual experience but require substantial production effort and viewing time; film recaps are shorter but depend on existing footage. Neither route directly provides a concise audiovisual account of a novel. We therefore study novel-to-recap video generation: producing a self-contained, source-grounded audiovisual retelling directly from a novel within a fixed viewing-time budget. This task requires compressing the story while preserving causal connections, allocating sufficient time to retained events, and aligning narration with newly generated visuals. We propose ReVi, a dual-loop multi-agent framework guided by edit first, generate second. Its Inner Loop plans story content, narration time, and corresponding shots before video generation. Across novels, its Outer Loop performs recursive self-improvement by revising both the editing policy and the meta policy that governs its revision. Experiments on two evaluation sets show that ReVi improves recap quality and duration compliance over representative baselines, with human ratings and multi-round improvement results providing further support.

title: A Tetration Distribution
summary: We introduce a one-parameter family of continuous distributions on the unit interval whose cumulative distribution functions are given by the odd-height power towers \(x\uparrow\uparrow n\) (\(n=1,3,5,\dots\)). The associated densities admit a simple recursive formula obtained by logarithmic differentiation. We prove that every such density is strictly positive on \((0,1)\) and integrates to one, thereby establishing that the construction yields a genuine probability distribution. Numerical investigation reveals a characteristic peak--dip--rise shape: a sharp mode lying just below \(e^{-e}\) for all examined heights, followed by a trough and a gradual recovery toward density value~1 at the right endpoint. We then identify the limiting distribution as the height tends to infinity through odd integers.

title: A Modular Open-Source Python Framework for Small Satellite Attitude Determination and Control
summary:
Advanced attitude determination and control (ADCS) techniques can be difficult for small satellite teams to adopt: tightly coupled implementations require substantial code changes to evaluate different actuators, sensors, orbits, mission goals, and control laws. Existing tools often emphasize orbit mechanics or flight software rather than closed-loop ADCS. This paper presents an open-source, modular ADCS framework in pure Python for rapid development, repeatable testing, and flight-oriented integration across heterogeneous spacecraft.
  The package supports torque- and command-level control, bound-respecting allocation, and full- and reduced-attitude objectives. Interchangeable estimation, control, planning, and actuator/sensor modules are reconfigured through configuration changes. Integrated simulation includes attitude and orbit propagation, sensor and actuator bias and noise, and environmental disturbances. An actuator-aware planner supports underactuated architectures, while hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) capability enables testing on mission-representative computers.
  Case studies include a 3U CubeSat with three magnetorquers and one reaction wheel, a magnetorquer-only 1U, and a 6U with three reaction wheels and thrusters. These demonstrate actuator and sensor failures, full- and reduced-attitude goals, and momentum management. HIL testing on a Raspberry Pi uses the same package. Adapting a published control law to a new actuator configuration requires fewer than five lines of configuration changes. The framework underpins flight software for an Earth-observing CubeSat with visible and long-wave infrared imagers, three magnetorquers, and one reaction wheel, without star trackers or propulsion.

title: Learning Directional Randers Geometry for Latent-Space Exploration
summary: Deep neural networks extract powerful latent representations from images, enabling fast and efficient downstream analysis. However, these latent spaces lack explicit geometric structure, leading to possibly poor interpolation fidelity and misleading extrapolation. Latent interpolation techniques assume symmetric transition costs which are often not the case for real world data. Their symmetric nature cannot capture directional processes, such as disease progression, where certain transitions are impossible (e.g. tumor growth dynamics or cognitive improvement in Alzheimer's disease). Although Riemannian metrics extend Euclidean geometry by incorporating curvature, they remain symmetric. We show that understanding asymmetry and not curvature alone directly addresses these problems. To do so we propose a new Finsler-Randers metric learning framework. It incorporates direction-dependent distances, thus enabling the computation of trajectories respecting monotonic sequential constraints. We demonstrate its potential for interpolation and extrapolation on controlled cross-sectional datasets.

title: A generalized lasso formulation of weighted and regularized (nearly-)isotonic regression on graphs
summary: In this paper we study a regularized version of nearly-isotonic regression with respect to a general partial order. In this estimator the sum of squares is weighted, with some of the weights allowed to be zero, and an additional quadratic penalty is imposed. The only assumption we make is that the quadratic part of the objective function is strictly convex, and we show that this assumption is mild. First, we show that for all sufficiently large values of the penalty parameter the estimator coincides with the regularized isotonic regression, in which the penalty is replaced by the isotonic constraint. Further, we prove that the resulting problem can be written as a generalized lasso problem with a design matrix of full column rank and with the penalty matrix unchanged. Next, we derive the dual problem, which is a quadratic program with box constraints, and write it in a sparse form that can be solved by standard quadratic programming solvers for sparse problems.

title: A Novel Conditional Adversarial Diffusion Model for High-Fidelity OCT-to-OCT Image Translation and Precise Anti-VEGF Therapy Response Prediction in Diabetic Macular Edema
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
summary: Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of severe vision loss among working-age adults. Although intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections currently serve as the first-line therapy for DME, a notable subset of patients fails to respond despite the substantial cost and clinical burden, suggesting they may benefit more from alternative interventions. Automated, noninvasive pre-treatment response assessment could therefore spare non-responders from the current trial-and-error treatment paradigm. In this study, we propose a novel conditional adversarial diffusion framework that synthesizes post-treatment optical coherence tomography (OCT) images from baseline scans, enabling the derivation of each patient's initial response to anti-VEGF therapy. The model was developed with subject-level 5-fold cross-validation on a US cohort (n = 127) and externally validated on an independent Iranian cohort (n = 44). Benchmarked against fourteen baseline and state-of-the-art translation models, the proposed model achieved the best treatment-response prediction performance among the methods evaluated for that task on both cohorts, with balanced accuracies of 85.7% and 93.0% on the US cohort and 85.2% and 95.3% on the external Iranian cohort at the 10% and 20% central subfield thickness reduction thresholds, respectively. Ultimately, this framework offers a decision-support tool to help ophthalmologists anticipate initial anti-VEGF outcomes in DME prior to treatment initiation, toward personalized therapy selection. The source code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
summary: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning reorganizes it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

title: Minimax signal detection in regression under differential privacy
summary: We establish minimax separation rates across sparsity levels for regression signal detection under $(ε, δ)$-central differential privacy, considering linear regression with an unknown error distribution and generalised linear models (GLMs) with an unknown intercept. Without sparsity restrictions, the separation rates for linear regression and GLMs with binary responses match the private Gaussian mean testing rate up to polylogarithmic factors. For GLMs with more than two possible response outcomes, additional information in the marginal response distribution permits faster detection of sufficiently small signals when the dimension exceeds the sample size $n$. Our upper bounds are based on a reduction to private mean testing, tests of dependence between the response and sparse covariate projections, and a response-only test that is adjusted for the unknown intercept. The resulting procedure adapts to unknown sparsity and matches our lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. We also construct polynomial-time tests that attain these rates when $ε\gtrsim n^{-1/2}$, and compare their numerical performance with existing private procedures.

title: Positioning and Radiation Efficiency Degrees of Freedom in Cascaded Pinching-Antenna Arrays
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to the IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
summary: In a pinching-antenna system (PASS), a single source feeds multiple pinches, resulting in a cascade that couples their radiated powers. A shared radiated-power limit, such as the interference power constraint in an underlay cognitive radio network, couples them again. We study such a network where PASS serves the secondary users. First, we formulate the joint optimization problem of the two degrees of freedom (DoF), pinch positions and radiation efficiencies, and characterize the single-link optimum analytically. Then, rather than proposing one method, we present the results for a grid of schemes whose two axes are the two DoF. Under an order-free attribution, positioning is worth 1.34 times radiation efficiency, and the two are near-perfect substitutes. We also show that substitutability is due to the constraint and not the cascade, since relaxing the constraint by 20 dB removes 97% of their interaction. At the joint reference, not knowing the primary receiver (PR) location costs 6.23 bit/s/Hz, more than twice the 2.87 that optimizing both DoF is worth. Instantaneous fading information adds a further 0.29 bit/s/Hz. Allocating efficiencies at equally spaced positions reaches 98% of the joint reference at about three orders of magnitude less computation.

title: LOLPlay: Benchmarking Real-Time Visual Agents in League of Legends
summary: Visual agents need to coordinate reasoning and action while their environment evolves during inference. We introduce LOLPlay, a benchmark in native \emph{League of Legends} with 36 champion-specific tasks spanning resource management, combat, cooperation, and objectives. Agents interact through screenshots and mouse--keyboard actions; automated initialization and 82 executable subgoal checks distinguish partial progress from completion. Across 324 task evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate of 25.0\% at low and medium effort, and the highest subgoal success rate of 40.3\% at medium effort. However, high effort improves neither metric over low effort for any model. For Astra, longer requests leave fewer interaction rounds, suggesting a cost to additional reasoning in real-time control. Trajectories reveal incomplete subgoal composition and actions executing after the observed scene changes, motivating agents that combine visual reasoning with timely action.

title: Terrain-Surface-Area Cover from LiDAR: Inverse-Probability-Weighted Estimation and a Global Cramér-von Mises Lack-of-Fit Test
comment: 32 pages, 6 tables, 3 figures. Synthetic validation; Lean 4 formal core. No real LiDAR or field data in this version
summary: Canopy cover is normally reported as a fraction of a horizontal map plane. When the domain of inference is the land surface, the appropriate target is the fraction of terrain surface area under canopy. We define this estimand on a C1 graph surface and show that it differs from vertical-projection cover by the planimetric covariance of cover with the area density, divided by the mean area density; the rumple index is a different quantity. A LiDAR pulse is recorded as a canopy return only when detection succeeds, so the naive return fraction estimates cover multiplied by the canopy detection probability. We study an inverse-probability-weighted estimator that uses that probability as the inclusion probability, and a weighted corner-averaged Cramér-von Mises lack-of-fit statistic for constant mean surface-area cover under independent canopy returns, calibrated by a parametric bootstrap. Synthetic validation on the flat plane and the Gaussian hill gives a naive bias near -0.40 and a weighted bias near 0.00; at 5000 pulses the test holds size at 0.02-0.06 across the simulated null cells and reaches power 0.79 under surface-uniform and 0.85 under plane-uniform sampling against broad slope-dependent cover, but only 0.12-0.13 against a compact hotspot. The definitions and their exact reductions are machine-checked in Lean 4. No field data yet.

title: When Music Needs Meaning: Semantic Communication as a Transformative Enabler for the Musical Metaverse
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted and Presented at IEEE International Symposium on the Internet of Sounds (IS2) Conference 2026
summary: The Musical Metaverse (MM) enables geographically distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents to interact through synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, imposing latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability requirements that are difficult to satisfy with conventional bit-level communication. This paper argues that semantic communication, understood here as the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, provides a principled communication paradigm for the MM. We define the MM from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific require ments; propose a three-pillar framework for musical semantic communication comprising semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization; survey representative work across semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, identifying the gaps that prevent their integration; and propose a semantic-first reference architecture based on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal semantic synchronization. The resulting framework positions the MM as a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.

title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
summary: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.

title: Nonparametric GARCH: An Iterated Neural Estimator
summary: We study nonparametric estimation and forecasting for GARCH-type processes and propose an iterated neural estimator that alternates between estimating the recursion map and updating the unobserved conditional variances. Under mild conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for the time-averaged in-sample variance-path error and show that the estimator is minimax rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Under stationarity and mixing conditions, we establish the same rate for recursion-map estimation and derive finite-sample bounds for out-of-sample variance forecasts and expected excess Gaussian quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss. The convergence rates depend on the true lag orders and remain unchanged when the fitted orders are overspecified. Simulation studies illustrate the effectiveness of our estimators under nonlinear and time-varying volatility dynamics. Real-data applications suggest that our neural methods perform competitively and can incorporate option-price and high-frequency information.

title: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable Agent for Blind Restoration of Multi-Artifact 3-D MRI
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ISBI 2027
summary: A brain MRI scan can carry an unknown mix of artifacts, so restoration has to be blind, yet most deep-learning methods are built to correct one known artifact. We present Dx-Rx, an agent in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) measures suspected artifacts before it repairs them. To our knowledge, it is the first agent to restore whole 3-D MRI volumes, whereas earlier MRI agents restore 2-D slices. In a loop, it looks at slices of the 3-D volume, calls five diagnostic tools (noise, spike, ghosting, bias field, motion) and four restoration tools in any order it chooses, checks each repair, can return to any earlier version to change the order, and ends with a radiology-style report of its diagnostic reasons, the repairs it applied and their results. We simulated up to five artifacts on 148 whole 3-D T1-weighted volumes, at levels calibrated to radiologists' grades of real scans. An MLLM that only looked at the image, as earlier MRI agents do, removed at most 19.7 % of the artifact error. With the best of five MLLMs, Dx-Rx removed a mean 64.5 %, nearly matching the 64.6 % of the same tools given the ground-truth artifacts, which are never known for a clinical scan. With all five models, it made no volume worse and was on par with or better than an expert rule-based pipeline built from the same tools (62.3 %). Code and demo are public at https://itu-biai.github.io/measure-before-you-repair.

title: A Compact Formula-Aware Spreadsheet Abstraction for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist spreadsheet users with tasks such as spreadsheet model construction, formula generation, and data analysis, yet their interaction with real-world spreadsheets remains limited by the mismatch between the structure of spreadsheets and the sequential textual representations typically provided to LLMs. We propose a compact formula-aware spreadsheet abstraction that represents large homogeneous ranges through their positions, types, R1C1 formula patterns, and selected boundary values. An efficient algorithm detects and structures these ranges before a textual serialization is supplied to an LLM. The abstraction is provided to the LLM before detailed spreadsheet content is submitted, improving the accuracy and efficiency of spreadsheet processing while reducing token consumption. We evaluate the method on 50 spreadsheet-query cases. The evaluation shows that the abstraction alone was sufficient to answer some queries. When additional spreadsheet content is required, the abstraction reduces the amount of data that must be submitted to the LLM, thereby reducing token consumption. The abstraction layer also improves the reliability and accuracy of spreadsheet processing. We conclude by discussing further techniques for combining spreadsheet static analysis with artificial intelligence to improve the reliability, accuracy, and efficiency of AI assisted spreadsheet tasks.

title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
summary: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Nonlinear Registration on Longitudinal PET Analysis in a Rodent Stroke Model
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Security and Networking (CAISN 2026)
summary: Longitudinal rodent positron emission tomography (PET) studies of stroke and neuromodulation rely on accurate registration to a common atlas space to detect group-level effects. Prior work applying ultra-high frequency low-intensity magnetic stimulation (UHF-LiMS) to a rat model of chronic capsule infarct used affine normalization to a Sprague Dawley MRI template without evaluating that choice. We compare a two-stage (affine and nonlinear) pipeline against an affine- only one for rat PET-to-atlas alignment on the same dataset. Across 32 longitudinal [18F]-FDG PET scans (8 rats, 4 timepoints), the nonlinear stage gave a higher Dice similarity coefficient on every scan, and the gain was significant at the rat level. Jacobian determinants showed no folding on the sampling grid. Group-level linear mixed-effects maps of change from baseline (AFNI 3dLME), computed identically under both pipelines, differ in the size, number and location of their suprathreshold clusters. In this dataset, the registration pipeline is therefore a variable that can change the interpretation of downstream group-level analyses.

title: InterceptFuzz: Interception-based Stateful Fuzzing of Single-Process Targets
summary: Stateful protocol implementations are commonly fuzzed by tools that act as a network client and exchange messages with the target over sockets. Some wireless and IoT protocol stacks instead provide a single-process simulation platform, in which all nodes run in one binary and exchange packets in memory. Such simulations are deterministic and fast, which suits fuzzing, but offer no socket to which existing stateful fuzzers can attach. Meanwhile, fuzzing infrastructure such as Google's OSS-Fuzz supports only stateless engines. This paper presents InterceptFuzz, a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process targets on top of an unmodified stateless fuzzing engine. InterceptFuzz requires only a hook where the target passes packets between nodes. Through this hook, it records benign traffic and injects fuzzed packets. It organizes the observed packet sequences in a Prefix Tree. Each seed carries a State ID that selects a node of this tree, and InterceptFuzz deterministically replays the recorded prefix before delivering the mutated packet. The tree grows with newly discovered sequences, while redundant states are pruned to keep its growth in check. InterceptFuzz powered by AFL++ is evaluated on the Nexus test framework of OpenThread and on the LTE and Wi-Fi models of ns-3, against an interception-based adaptation of AFLNet and against Concat, an AFL++-based baseline that mutates a whole message sequence as one input. On OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, InterceptFuzz covers significantly more branches than both baselines. Seven previously unknown crash signatures were found in OpenThread. Concat, despite its simplicity, covers more branches than AFLNet in every campaign on OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, and on OpenThread it exposes the same crash signatures as InterceptFuzz, although some of them in fewer campaigns.

title: Two-Layer Random ReLU Networks Can Separate Disjoint Classes
summary:
