The proof uses only identities over finite fields, the characteristic polynomial of a $2\times2$ matrix, and elementary properties of Frobenius automorphisms. The repeated-root case and all parity cases are considered separately. It follows that the derivative of each function has kernel of size two in every nonzero direction, and hence both $F_2$ and $F_3$ are APN for every admissible $m$.

title: Faster Planar Diameter using Pseudoline Envelopes
summary:
We give an improved algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ time algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter of Gawrychowski, Kaplan, Mozes, Sharir, and Weimann [SIAM J. Comput. 2021] and the recent $\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})$ time algorithm for unweighted undirected planar diameter of Fredslund-Hansen, Mozes, and Weimann [SOSA 2027].
  The main new result is an improved data structure for computing the farthest vertex when given feasible planar distances to the vertices on the outer face. The critical insight is the fact that normalized distances to the vertices of a face behave like pseudolines, for which we can leverage range searching and upper envelope data structures. Using the farthest vertex data structure, we are able to compute all vertex eccentricities and diameter in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$.

title: Nearly-Linear Query Algorithm for Submodular Maximization subject to a Matroid Constraint
summary:
We consider monotone submodular maximization subject to a matroid constraint. The seminal continuous greedy algorithm of Calinescu, Chekuri, Pál, and Vondrák~[SICOMP'11] achieves the tight approximation of $(1-1/e)$. Since then, a line of works by Badanidiyuru and Vondrák~[SODA'14], Buchbinder, Feldman, and Schwartz~[SODA'15 \& MOR'17], Kobayashi and Terao~[ICALP'24], Buchbinder and Feldman~[FOCS'24 \& SICOMP'25], and Buchbinder and Feldman~[STOC'25] has developed efficient $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for this problem.
  We present a combinatorial randomized $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that requires $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(n)$ independence-oracle and value-oracle queries, where $n$ is the number of elements in the matroid. This is the first $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm with both independence-oracle and value-oracle query complexities nearly-linear in $n$ and polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$. To achieve this, we develop a new local search algorithm, which we call \emph{protected local search}, based on the potential function of Buchbinder and Feldman~[FOCS'24 \& SICOMP'25].

title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
summary: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

title: HiLo-WAM: Decoupling Long-Horizon Task Evolution and Local Dynamics in World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.

title: RGB Photo Enhancement with Deep Learning on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
summary: On-device RGB photo enhancement is a popular task that is needed for quality improvement of photos captured with mobile devices as well as for retouching of images acquired through other sources. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose participants to design fast solutions that can perform comprehensive enhancement of RGB photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale DPED dataset consisting of RGB image pairs captured with an old iPhone 3GS smartphone and a professional Canon 70D DSLR camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to enhance Full HD resolution RGB images on both platforms under 300 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

title: A Unified Isoparametric Moving Mesh PDE Method for P1 and Q1 Elements with Certified Local Nonsingularity
summary: We develop a unified isoparametric moving mesh partial differential equation (MMPDE) method for $P_1$ simplicial and $Q_1$ tensor-product elements, including elements on embedded surfaces. Mesh movement follows a prescribed symmetric positive-definite metric through equidistribution and alignment. For $Q_1$ elements, we prove that bounded, exactly integrated adaptation energy prevents local Jacobian rank loss on a fixed finite mesh at sharp critical exponents. The result also gives local full-rank preservation for embedded bilinear surface elements. A complete physical-coordinate gradient accounts for metric variation at moving quadrature points. For the discrete MMPDE, we use whole-element validity tests and develop sufficient Bernstein certificates for trilinear hexahedra. An explicit positive-margin bound on each fixed stage is provided by an optional certificate barrier. Numerical examples illustrate metric-driven movement on one-dimensional, planar, volume, and graph-surface meshes. Limitations of pointwise hexahedral Jacobian sampling are also presented.

title: Haptic Shared Control for Multi-Robot Systems
comment: PhD thesis, Université de Rennes (IRISA UMR 6074 / Inria Rennes), defended 30 April 2025. 134 pages, 38 figures
summary: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators. We propose a modification of the global connectivity maintenance algorithm to incorporate measurements taken in agent's local frame, using sensors with limited fields of view. This algorithm, responsible for the autonomous behavior of the multi-robot system, is combined with different adaptive supervision strategies, allowing the user to exert control at varying scales over the entire group. (i) Single Agent Control (S): The operator directly controls a single robot, (ii) Pinning Control (P): The operator imposes constraints on multiple robots to influence the group, (iii) Centroid Control (C): The operator acts on the system's center of mass to steer the entire fleet. In conjunction with the connectivity maintenance algorithm, these methods ensure compliance with inter-agent constraints while providing haptic feedback to the user regarding the system's connectivity state. The effectiveness of these approaches was evaluated through a user study, comparing performance with and without haptic feedback across multiple scenarios tailored to the different control modes.

title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
summary: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

title: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
summary: Interpretability often locates concepts by copying part of a language model's state from one input into another (activation patching). A larger output change counts as stronger evidence that this part carries the concept. Methods that learn which part to copy often change the output more than the whole state does. By that reading, learned parts isolate the concept more cleanly. Yet the whole contains the part. So whose effect is this excess, the network's or the method's? Copying the whole state learns nothing, so it shows what the network produces. We prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole. A part therefore exceeds the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, which does not require isolating the concept more cleanly. Objectives that reward a larger effect select such parts. Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites. In both, changing only its objective to target what the network produces removes most of the excess. It therefore comes largely from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence.

title: Federated Transfer Learning for Medical Image Classification under Mixed Skew
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures and 2 tables. Presented at 4th IEEE International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2026)
summary: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target. On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while reducing inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline, yielding accuracy and cross-client equity jointly. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Alexandre-Leclercq/PAFP.

title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

title: Matchings under One-Sided Preferences with Soft Quotas
summary: Assigning applicants to posts in the presence of applicant preferences and quotas associated with posts is extensively investigated. For a post, a lower quota guarantees, and an upper quota limits the number of applicants assigned to it. Typically, quotas are assumed to be fixed, which need not be the case in practice. We address this by introducing a soft quota setting, in which every post is associated with two values - lower target and upper target - which together denote a range for the intended number of applicants in any assignment. Unlike the fixed quota setting, we allow the number of applicants assigned to a post to fall outside the range. This leads to assignments with deviation. Here, we study the problem of computing an assignment that has two orthogonal optimization objectives - minimizing the deviation (maximum or total) with respect to soft quotas and ensuring optimality with respect to preferences of applicants (rank-maximality or fairness). The order in which these objectives are considered, the different possibilities to optimize deviation combined with the well-studied notions of optimality with respect to preferences open up a range of optimization problems of practical importance. We present efficient algorithms based on flow networks to solve these optimization problems. We also consider a generalization of the soft quota setting, where every deviation is associated with a cost. We show extensions of our algorithms for solving the problems in this setting.

title: The Power of Interaction in Locally Edge-Private Subgraph Counting
summary:
We study (non-induced) subgraph counting under interactive local edge differential privacy (LEDP). Given a fixed pattern graph $H$ with $k$ vertices, $\ell\ge1$ edges, and $q$ connected components, our goal is to approximately count its copies in an arbitrary $n$-vertex undirected graph while preserving edge privacy.
  We give two complementary accuracy guarantees. First, for every $H$, we give Linear Noise Cancellation (LNC), a two-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error and root mean square error both $O(n^{k-3/2}/\varepsilon^\ell)$ on every $n$-vertex graph. For fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, this improves the optimal noninteractive additive error for triangles by a factor of $\sqrt n$ and gives the same improvement in worst-case root mean square error for all cliques on at least three vertices. To our knowledge, this is the first separation between interactive and noninteractive LEDP subgraph counting, showing that a single additional round can improve worst-case accuracy polynomially.
  Second, we determine how accuracy improves when the graph has maximum degree at most a public bound $d$. Our Predict and Correct (PC) framework gives an $(\ell+2)$-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error $O(n^{q-1/2}d^{k-q-1}\log^{3\ell-2}n/\varepsilon^\ell)$. For connected patterns, its polynomial factor is $\sqrt n\,d^{k-2}$, giving sublinear error on constant-degree graphs at fixed privacy. We prove matching lower bounds in $n$ and $d$, up to logarithmic factors at fixed privacy, even under arbitrary interaction and approximate privacy with sufficiently small $δ$. At $d=Θ(n)$, the lower bound also establishes the optimality of LNC's dependence on $n$.

title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
summary: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.

title: Positional Encoding is All You Need for Scalable Equivariance Constraint Relaxation
summary: Equivariant neural networks incorporate known symmetries of the data, such as permutations, rotations, or translations, directly into their architecture, often improving sample efficiency and generalization. However, strict equivariance can make optimization difficult, for example, when the data only approximately satisfy the assumed symmetry, or when the equivariance constraints induce a challenging loss landscape. Recent studies have shown that relaxing equivariance during training by introducing non-equivariant dense linear layers can ease optimization in such cases and improve the performance of the resulting strictly equivariant model, after removing the relaxation layers at test time. While effective, this approach incurs a significant computational overhead, limiting its applicability in scalable architectures. In this work, we propose a more efficient constraint-relaxation method based on positional encoding (PE). Our framework injects a positional encoding with learnable scale that breaks the model's original symmetry. This positional signal is gradually annealed to zero, recovering the original equivariant model by the end of training. Empirically, we demonstrate significant improvements for translational and rotational equivariant models with only marginal compute and memory overhead.

title: Effects of Parton Pair Correlations on Direct-Photon Yields and Elliptic Flow in Heavy-Ion Collisions
summary: Direct photons escape heavy-ion collisions with little rescattering, carrying information from the full emission history. Yet describing the measured direct-photon yield and the sizable elliptic flow $v_2$ together remains a long-standing challenge. Here we explore how correlations between emitting partons may affect both observables. The local $2\to2$ photon rate depends on the joint distribution of incoming partons, so a connected correlation between them can change photon emission without changing the one-particle distribution of medium particles. Once folded over the evolving medium in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions, the correlation raises the photon yield toward the fitted PHENIX and ALICE data and increases $v_2$ mainly at intermediate $p_T$. The fitted temperature dependence accounts for most of the net flow increase in this region, suggesting that the correlation changes the relative contributions between hotter and cooler regions.

title: Graph Similarity Meets Optimal Transport
summary:
A natural way to compare two graphs is to align their vertex sets by a bijection and to measure the difference of the aligned adjacency matrices in a matrix norm. Depending on the norm, this yields, for example, the edit distance, the cut distance, the spectral distance, and the local edit distance. To make these distances applicable to graphs of different order, one can consider blowups of the graphs or, equivalently, relax bijections to fractional alignments, that is, optimal transport plans between the uniform distributions on the vertex sets, in the spirit of Gromov-Wasserstein distances.
  We investigate how much the optimal transport versions can differ from their bijective counterparts, that is, we quantify their integrality gaps. For the edit distance, we improve the best known upper bound on the integrality gap from 3 to 2 and the lower bound from 6/5 to 4/3. For the cut distance, we approach Lovász's conjecture that $δ_\square \le 2δ_\square^{OT}$ from both sides. We improve the previously best known upper bound $δ_\square \le 32 \cdot (δ_\square^{OT})^{1/67}$ (Borgs, Chayes, Lovász, Sós and Vesztergombi, Adv. Math. 2008) to $δ_\square \le C_\varepsilon \cdot (δ_\square^{OT})^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, and we construct graphs $G,H$ with $δ_\square(G,H) = 2δ_\square^{OT}(G,H)$, establishing a factor-2 lower bound that matches Lovász's conjecture. For the local edit and spectral distances, we obtain upper bounds of order $\sqrt{t\ln(1/t)}$ and $\sqrt{t}$, respectively, where $t$ is the corresponding optimal transport distance, and we show that, unlike for the edit and cut distances, no linear upper bounds are possible.
  Finally, we show that computing the optimal transport distances is NP-hard, and we give hardness of approximation results for the cut, spectral, and local edit distances.

title: Equal Access, Unequal Gains? GitHub Copilot and Productivity Among Developers with Disabilities
summary: Generative AI tools are increasingly used in software development and have been associated with benefits such as faster task completion and improved perceived productivity. However, whether these benefits extend across different developer populations remains unclear. This is especially relevant for developers with disabilities, whose work can already be impacted by accessibility barriers. Yet, evidence remains limited across a broader range of disability groups. This study investigates whether the wider availability of GitHub Copilot is associated with changes in productivity among GitHub users who self-identify as having a disability. Using publicly available profile and repository data, we curated a dataset of 199 developers across multiple disability groups and compared their activity before and after GitHub Copilot became freely available. We found that most disability groups showed a descriptive pattern of fewer commits but more code modified. In several disability groups, the distribution of developers across commit activity levels shifted toward both lower and higher level, leaving fewer developers at moderate level. However, we found no evidence that changes in commits or net lines modified differed across disability groups. These findings suggest that the wider availability of GitHub Copilot cannot be associated with a broad increase or decrease in observable development activity, while patterns of change varied across developers and disability groups.

title: Do Agentic Policies Need to Look at Every Step? Geometric Abstraction for Reasoning and Action
comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Agentic Robotics. 13 pages, 8 figures. Project page: https://geometric-abstraction.github.io
summary: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.

title: Rank-metric intersecting codes
summary:
Intersecting codes are codes in which any two nonzero codewords share a common nonzero coordinate, and they have been extensively studied due to their applications in communication theory, cryptography, and combinatorics. Recently, geometric interpretations have provided new insights into intersecting codes, both in the Hamming metric and, more recently, in the rank metric for linear codes.
  In this paper, we introduce and study matrix rank-metric intersecting codes. By defining the support of a matrix as its row space, we extend the notion of intersecting codes to the matrix rank-metric setting. Using the slice space associated with the generator tensor of a rank-metric code, we derive a geometric characterization that is equivalent to the intersecting property. This characterization generalizes the known results for linear rank-metric intersecting codes and highlights both analogies and differences with the linear case. In particular, it yields bounds on the parameters of intersecting codes, one of which is sharp and differs from the one in the linear case, together with first constructions. We then consider codes that are closed under multiplication, i.e. matrix algebras. In this setting, the intersecting property can be read off from the algebraic structure, namely the Jacobson radical and the socle. This provides a simple and flexible way to construct many intersecting codes, including codes that do not satisfy the classical sufficient condition on the minimum distance.

title: Semi-Streaming Reachability and Shortest Paths in $n^{1/3+o(1)}$ Passes
summary:
In the semi-streaming model, the edges of an $n$-vertex graph arrive in a stream, and an algorithm makes multiple passes over that stream while using only $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space. The number of passes needed to compute single-source reachability in directed graphs is a long-standing open question in streaming algorithms, going back to Henzinger, Raghavan, and Rajagopalan (1998). The best known semi-streaming algorithm uses $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ passes due to Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford (2019), while the best lower bound is $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$ passes due to Guruswami and Onak (2016).
  We give streaming algorithms for computing single-source reachability and shortest paths on $n$-vertex directed graphs using $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space and $n^{1/3+o(1)}$ passes. Our algorithms are based on implicit hopsets, which are large hopsets that can be represented implicitly in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space. We introduce this notion and give new constructions for implicit hopsets with small hopbound. Along the way, we obtain new work-depth tradeoffs for parallel shortest paths in directed graphs, improving the recent result of Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak (2026).

title: FloMo: 3D Scene Flow as a World Action Model Intermediate for Learning from Human Video
summary: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.

title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity
comment: 27 pages, 19 figures, 17 tables; 9-page supplementary material appended. Submitted to Composite Structures. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23512947
summary: Periodic composites with cohesive interfaces and matrix plasticity require nonlinear cell solutions in multiscale analysis. Process-zone condensation eliminates the linear elastic remainder of the cell by a Schur complement, retaining all interfacial and process-zone internal variables. Influence matrices recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent. One back-substitution per increment checks that the matrix outside the retained zone remains elastic. While this holds, the reduction is exact relative to the full discretisation, also with a plastic matrix, and requires no training. In an E-glass/epoxy cell, eight of nine two-dimensional paths agree with the full cell to 1e-11 in stress and tangent; the check flags the ninth. Three paths on each of two three-dimensional meshes need zone expansion. Excluding setup and checks, two-dimensional path timings show an aggregate speed-up of 3.3; certified three-dimensional zones show none. In adaptive finite element squared (FE$^2$) simulations of a perforated plate, the reduced solver reproduces the full-cell response within solver tolerances, 1.51 times faster for glass/polypropylene and slower for glass/epoxy. Independent Ansys models agree to below 1e-3 in cell stress and about 0.6% in plate reactions, although local damage and plasticity onsets differ. The advantage depends on zone size, active set and adaptation costs.

title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models
summary: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.

title: Dataset Recommendation for Heterogeneous and Dynamic Scholarly Graphs via Multimodal Representation Learning
summary: Researchers struggle to find relevant datasets amid the growing volume of data across repositories and scholarly publications. Manual dataset retrieval is time-consuming and often fails to identify valuable resources that are not easily discoverable through direct links or popularity metrics. Dataset recommendation, which aims to identify datasets relevant to a paper, author, or query, has become essential for improving dataset discoverability and reuse. However, this task remains challenging because Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) are large-scale, heterogeneous, dynamic, and incomplete. Although openly available SKGs organize scientific knowledge by linking scholarly outcomes, they often lack meaningful connections between datasets, leaving them isolated and underutilized. These graphs contain millions of evolving relations but still suffer from missing or inaccurate metadata, duplicate records, and weak dataset integration. This work presents the Multimodal Scholarly Attention Network (MM-SAN), a heterogeneous multimodal graph representation learning method for recommending datasets relevant to research publications within real-world SKGs. MM-SAN combines topology-aware and text-based embeddings, enabling effective recommendations even when textual metadata is limited or absent. It operates in transductive, semi-inductive, and fully inductive settings, adapting to evolving SKGs without requiring retraining. Experiments show that MM-SAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, providing a robust and scalable solution for dataset recommendation.

title: Trajectory Evaluation via Rollout-Free World Model for End-to-end Autonomous Driving
summary: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Toward Constant-Factor Maximin Share Guarantees for Subadditive Valuations
summary:
For $n$ agents and $m$ indivisible goods, an agent's maximin share (MMS) is the largest minimum bundle value she can obtain by partitioning the goods into $n$ bundles. Constant MMS approximations are known for additive, submodular, or XOS valuations, but whether such a guarantee exists for general subadditive valuations remains open. We advance this question in two directions. For general subadditive valuations, we exponentially improve the guarantee from $Ω(1/\log\log n)$ to $Ω(1/\log^* n)$, where $\log^* n$ is the iterated logarithm. We then seek constant MMS guarantees under additional structure on subadditive valuations by studying $q$-partitioning valuations: every partition of a bundle into at most $q$ groups admits nonnegative group prices that sum to the bundle's value and whose sum on any collection of groups is at most the value of their union. This hierarchy ranges from subadditivity at $q=2$ to XOS for $q\ge m$. We give the first study of MMS in the intermediate classes and prove constant guarantees whenever $q/n$ has a fixed positive lower bound, including $1/6$ for $q\ge n$ and $1/4$ for $q\ge2n$. For XOS valuations, we further improve the universal guarantee from $4/17\approx 0.2353$ to $5/16=0.3125$.
  For subadditive valuations, we prove a bidding amplification theorem that gives an exponential bound on each agent's probability of receiving less than half her MMS, while satisfying her budget in every outcome. For $q$-partitioning valuations, we give a scalar criterion that converts bounds on the value lost from disjoint deletions within a bundle into bounds on potential losses, even when an agent contributes zero below the target bundle value. For XOS valuations, we prove a reservation theorem that selects goods for integral assignment together with auxiliary additive valuations and accounts for the loss in rounding.

title: Nested Field-of-View Barriers for Teleoperated Multi-Robot Relay Chains
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the American Control Conference (ACC)
summary: Teleoperation of mobile robots in communication-denied environments requires maintaining a communication link while allowing the operator to maneuver freely. We propose a shared-autonomy framework in which a teleoperated leader is followed by a chain of autonomous robots that relays a line of sight to a fixed base station, a geometric proxy for the link. Connectivity is enforced geometrically through visibility-based Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), with each agent computing its control input locally through a quadratic program. A strict visibility constraint guarantees connectivity, but a follower with no independent motion objective remains stationary, stalling the leader at the boundary of the safe set. Relaxing it preserves mobility at the cost of the guarantee. Our framework resolves this conflict through nested hard-soft visibility constraints: a full field-of-view (FoV) constraint enforced strictly to guarantee connectivity and a contracted FoV constraint imposed on each follower as a relaxed behavioral objective that drives it inward before the connectivity boundary is reached. We prove feasibility of the local quadratic programs and forward invariance of the connected, collision-free set under the resulting distributed controller. The contraction parameter shapes follower behavior without affecting the guarantee, which follows from the strict constraint alone. The framework is evaluated in confined and cluttered environments on two simulated systems: a kinematic integrator and software-in-the-loop Crazyflie quadrotors. Compared with a baseline tuned to reach the goal in comparable time, the framework keeps the links far closer to the connected set and moves the followers less.

title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/

title: Characterizing Serverless Workloads: A Large-Scale Analysis of Function-as-a-Service Platforms
summary: Serverless computing is a popular approach to application deployment without having to manage the underlying infrastructure. Its most common implementation is Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), in which applications are structured as fine-grained functions. FaaS providers face non-trivial tasks in the management of their platforms, including cold starts, auto-scaling, and scheduling. The design of optimized platforms requires an accurate understanding of realistic serverless workloads. However, existing research and platforms rely on insights from single, often outdated datasets. In this work, we conduct a large-scale, cross-platform comparative analysis of eight publicly available FaaS workload traces from major cloud providers (Alibaba, Azure, Huawei, IBM) and a scientific computing platform (Globus). We provide a comprehensive and up-to-date view of the serverless ecosystem by characterizing key dimensions such as invocation patterns, latency, cold start behavior, and resource utilization. Our analysis shows that although invocation patterns remain universal, execution times have shortened, shifting the performance bottleneck toward platform scheduling and dependency management. We also observe an architectural shift toward "Serverless 2.0" models, where concurrent, long-lived containers are increasingly utilized to bypass cold start penalties. Furthermore, we found resource over-provisioning and extreme skew in user request volumes. These findings provide actionable insights for designing more efficient FaaS platforms, informing improved approaches to targeted cold start mitigation, predictive resource management, and dependency-aware scheduling.

title: Finding Hypercliques Faster Than Brute Force
summary:
We show that for any fixed $k$, there exists $\varepsilon_k > 0$ such that, given a $(k-1)$-uniform hypergraph $H$ on $n$ vertices, one can count the number of $k$-hypercliques in $H$ in $O(n^{k-\varepsilon_k})$ time. This refutes the hyperclique conjecture of Lincoln, Vassilevska Williams, and Williams (SODA 2018). Our result follows from the uniform construction of a family of arithmetic circuits of size $O(n^{k-\varepsilon_k})$ for the $k$-hyperclique tensor, a natural higher-order generalization of the matrix multiplication tensor.
  We obtain two corollaries. First, for every $k$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that Max-$k$SAT can be solved in $2^{(1-\varepsilon)n} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(m,n)$ time. Second, for every $k$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that arithmetic progressions of length $k$ in subsets of $\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$ can be detected in $n^{2-\varepsilon}$ time. Both corollaries refute other prominent conjectures in the literature.

title: Manifold Embedding of Deep Image Features for Image Matching via Neural Adjoint Maps
summary: Estimating semantic correspondences between different object instances of similar categories in real-world images is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. While the recent progress in foundation models has significantly advanced solutions for such difficult image correspondence problems, respective methods are often insufficiently regularised. For example, common nearest-neighbour matching with foundation model features often results in noisy correspondences, which is particularly prominent when solving for dense correspondences. In this work, we tackle image matching via functional maps, which have been popularised for 3D shape matching due to their powerful spectral formalism utilising an efficient low-dimensional linear representation. However, functional maps require that domains (in our cases the rectangular image grids) are equipped with an informative and non-trivial geometry. To define a meaningful manifold structure for images, we use Galerkin's method from finite elements to derive a discrete Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO) based on a manifold embedding of deep image features. Further, we leverage a neural adjoint map that allows to represent non-linear mappings. We demonstrate that our method sets the new state of the art among zero-shot image correspondence methods on multiple dense correspondence benchmarks of real-world images. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NafieAmrani/NAMI

title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
summary: Repeated robotic monitoring requires localization across visits to the same environment, even if the environment changes. Such changes can substantially reduce persistent visual content, and repetitive structures can lead to incorrect cross-session correspondences. In this paper, we address visual multi-session registration of a new data recording (the query session) to a previously reconstructed reference map. Under substantial visual and structural changes, cross-session localization may be possible only for parts of the trajectory. In our approach, we therefore rely on a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints and combine them with within-session relative-pose information to register the complete trajectory to the reference map. We first estimate absolute alignment hypotheses through visual place recognition, local feature matching, and geometric verification. We then use sequence consensus to reject hypotheses that are inconsistent with a common query-to-reference alignment and retain the remaining poses as absolute anchors. These anchors are refined through featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian feature field and combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a robust pose-graph optimization. We evaluate our approach on 15 cross-session experiments from the challenging HILTI26 construction-site dataset, covering substantial scene changes and difficult-to-match environments. Our method achieves 94.4% recall within 1m and 100.0% within 5m, outperforming independent image localization, which peaks at 65.3% and 70.7%, respectively, as well as direct registration of independently reconstructed Structure-from-Motion geometry. Our results show that sparse, reliable absolute anchors can provide accurate and complete trajectory registration even when reliable cross-session correspondences are available only for part of the query session.

title: LatentTriad: Pre-Action Risk Representations for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
comment: Preprint. Under review. 44 pages, 16 figures, 37 tables. 9 pages of main text
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly extended with reusable skills, but untrusted skill content can induce operations outside the user's task. Detecting this contextual risk requires more than suspicious-pattern matching, while dynamic analysis incurs the cost of skill execution. We find that hidden states formed during prefill contain readable information about task-operation consistency, including across held-out expression forms in controlled evaluations. Matched Operation-state interventions also affect later Boundary states and shift fixed risk readouts toward the donor label. Based on these findings, we introduce LatentTriad, which combines contextual Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions, and departures from benign state relationships. All branches share one prefill: detection generates no output tokens, invokes no tools, and executes no skill code. Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbones, LatentTriad achieves 99.0-99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0-94.6% source-macro F1. A separately measured compact implementation completes prefill and detection in a median of 259-284 ms. These results connect pre-action risk readability and functional influence to execution-free skill screening.

title: Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs
summary:
We study automated design of strategyproof (SP) mechanisms for randomized facility location on continuous metric graphs, with the objective of minimizing total distance. We develop methods for computing upper and lower bounds on the optimal approximation ratio achievable by SP mechanisms for a given graph and number of agents.
  For the lower bound, we propose a cost-preserving reduction to a finite domain that yields lower bounds for unrestricted SP mechanisms through linear programming dual certificates.
  For the upper bound, we introduce finite representations of mechanisms, called piecewise-linear attributions (PL attributions), that mix piecewise-linear deterministic mechanisms using affine weights on a triangulation of the report space. We show that for mechanisms represented by PL attributions, checking SP and an approximation guarantee reduces to finitely many quadratic nonnegativity tests over compact polytopes. With exact arithmetic and comparisons, each verification certifies the proposed property or returns locations where it fails. In addition, we introduce a strengthening of the incentive notion called strong strategyproofness. We show that for fixed component mechanisms and regions of a PL attribution, the strong strategyproofness requirement can be expressed by a finite number of linear constraints on the attribution coefficients. Using these theoretical results, we propose a heuristic procedure for computing an upper bound on the approximation ratio.
  We compute certified upper and lower bounds on several metric graphs and numerically evaluate the proposed search procedure.
  Lastly, we show that deterministic SP onto mechanisms on graphs are strongly strategyproof and admit PL attributions. Thus restricting attention to strongly strategyproof mechanisms admitting PL attributions loses no deterministic SP onto mechanisms.

title: LoopQ: Fair, Closed-Loop Evaluation of Quantized Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision-language-action (VLA) models promises smaller and faster VLA deployments. However, when analyzing existing VLA quantization works, we realised that it is hard to reason about the performance of the suggested quantization method compared to existing, similar, or in many cases, simpler PTQ methods. We present LoopQ, a closed-loop benchmark that compares multiple quantization policies on the same checkpoint, layers and engine, varying only the method and the kernels. We evaluate RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant and QuantVLA on four VLAs with more than 180,000 episodes of LIBERO and LIBERO-plus, compare against QVLA's reported results on the same layers, and benchmark whether the four public VLA-quantization releases can be reproduced. We benchmark the methods on an NVIDIA H100, an L4, and a Jetson AGX Thor. Our results show that while quantization reliably saves memory, 2-3x for real low-bit models, VLA-specific PTQ methods underperform compared to simpler generic baselines. At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA, plain RTN matches the calibrated methods, and plain AWQ matches the success QVLA reports for itself. Standard LIBERO hides the losses that do exist: configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5-4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Speed is a weaker story. At batch 1 on the H100, no quantized pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT configuration is faster than its 16-bit model (1.06-1.58x slower on library kernels); only the L4 with int8 kernels gains (4-14%), the Thor is slower on every 4-bit configuration, and the engine alone changes latency by 2.1x. Profiling explains why: pi0.5's quantized backbone is compute-bound, while its memory-bound action expert, 63% of GPU time and 13% of the parameters, stays in 16 bits.

title: A Gated Spec-Driven Workflow: An Audit-Trail Study of Coding-Agent Work
summary: Spec-driven development (SDD) asks a coding agent to work from specifications, plans, and task lists rather than from the chat transcript. We study one such workflow for Claude Code, in which almost every control is an instruction carried out by the same model that it constrains. The user must approve each stage before the next begins. A reviewer subagent checks each artefact against a fixed, stage-specific defect list, and an executor subagent may only touch the files listed in its task. After each block of tasks, the orchestrator runs a file-inventory check to detect undeclared changes. We analyse the logs and transcripts of nine features in seven projects, all run by the authors, ranging from a Fortran solver and Python programs to books and this paper. Of these, five finished with every planned task done, including the Fortran solver feature, and 288 of the 581 planned tasks were completed block by block. The executor kept to its declared files: it left only one undeclared change in the deliverable folder, and the check caught it, although its reports record other departures from the protocol. The weak point was the orchestrator, which runs and judges its own checks. It recorded undeclared changes in 11 of 247 block checks, mostly from the authors' in-round requests and the environment, and stopped work in only four.

title: The Platonic Brain: Representational Convergence in EEG Foundation Models
summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) predicts that artificial neural networks converge on shared representations as scale and performance increase. We test whether these predictions hold for representations of the human brain with EEG foundation models. Using EEG recordings from six participants watching a television series, together with aligned visual and language content, we tested whether EEG foundation-model representations converge within and across modalities as their embeddings become better at decoding an informative set of EEG markers. We found that EEG models with greater decodability showed stronger cross-family alignment in both local neighbourhood similarity and global structure, not consistently increasing with model parameter count. Cross-modal convergence was modality and metric dependent: greater EEG decodability was associated with stronger global alignment to language, but not consistently to vision models, while local alignment showed no consistent association. This dissociation may reflect local sensitivity to low-level sensory features, whereas global geometry may capture weaker shared semantic structure.

title: Dual-VaDE: Efficient and Robust Prototype Learning via Variational Dual-Domain Mixture Priors
summary: In this paper, we propose Dual-VaDE, an unsupervised generative framework for learning interpretable anatomical prototypes from unlabeled medical images. In contrast to previous variational methods that rely on a single spatial latent code, which often entangles global geometry with local textures and fails to capture their cross-domain dependencies, Dual-VaDE introduces a dual-domain Gaussian mixture prior that explicitly couples spatial anatomy with phase-preserving Fourier spectral representations. We derive an exact, closed-form variational lower bound that fuses this joint prior into the decoder and optimizes the entire network end-to-end via an alternating EM formulation, avoiding heuristic two-stage clustering while ensuring superior training stability and robustness. Evaluated on OASIS-3 brain MRI, Dual-VaDE delivers substantially sharper and more plausible prototypes, achieves superior cluster separation with improvements of up to 94% over spatial-only baselines, exhibits markedly reduced variance across random seeds, and incurs negligible inference overhead (0.28 ms per image).

title: Molecular Prior Networks
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap
summary: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the predictive performance of the transformer model is only partially explained by simple molecular similarity.

title: Workload-Static Optical Circuit Switching For Scalable LLM Inference Decode
summary: LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
summary: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.

title: HLO-AMP: Hierarchical Loco-Manipulation from Object-Aware Motion Priors
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). Video: https://youtu.be/viR_ULnRDQQ
summary: Hierarchical pipelines for humanoid loco-manipulation typically pair a task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC) with a downstream task policy. Such WBCs are often trained through manual reward shaping, which yields visibly machine-like motions; more consequentially, they are trained without the manipulated object in the scene. Object dynamics are instead approximated through randomized end-effector force disturbances, a proxy that fails to reproduce the distributed multi-contact wrench a real payload applies across the arms and torso, with the gap becoming critical near the platform's payload limit. In this work, we train the low-level (LL) controller itself as an object-aware motion prior: a single policy trained via motion imitation on retargeted motion-capture (MoCap) references that span the core motion primitives of the downstream task, with the manipulated object physically present in the scene. This single stage inherits natural human-like coordination from the references and absorbs the realistic contact wrench at its source, while exposing the same compact task-space command interface used by command-tracking WBCs. A reference-free high-level (HL) policy is then trained on top, with its action channel anchored to the empirical envelope of the low-level training data so that it generalizes the priors to a long-horizon multi-stage task while structurally preventing queries that would push the low level off-distribution. We instantiate the framework on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place: the same deployed policy generalizes across object masses and dimensions, initial and goal poses, and reactively recovers from intentional drops mid-carry. Video: https://youtu.be/viR_ULnRDQQ.

title: Distributed Linear Bandits for Freshness-Aware Preprocessing in MEC-Enabled Digital Twin Networks
summary: Digital twins (DTs) require timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices to accurately represent the state of the corresponding physical systems, but transmitting large data volumes can compromise freshness. Moreover, different task classes have distinct computational demands and freshness requirements, while stochastic task generation and sizes complicate resource allocation. In this paper, we propose a freshness-aware framework in which multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data, reducing transmission volume and DT-server processing load. The framework establishes mutual support between DT and MEC servers. The DTs determine feasible CPU-allocation strategies guaranteeing class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements under specified workload, delay, and update-generation bounds. MEC servers collaboratively identify the feasible strategy minimizing expected freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. We formulate CPU-strategy selection as a fixed-confidence distributed best-arm identification problem in linear bandits, with MEC servers as agents and CPU allocations across task classes as arms. We employ DistLinGapE, a distributed collaborative learning method, to coordinate exploration and share observations. Numerical results show that the method identifies the optimal feasible strategy and reduces preprocessing delay when deployed under stationary task-class assignments and workload statistics. Collaboration yields an identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers in the evaluated settings.

title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand-object configurations to emerge implicitly. We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand-object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist. DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks. These results show that explicit hand-object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation. More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.

title: An Investigation on Numerical Bugs in GPU Programs Towards Automated Bug Detection
comment: Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), ISSTA 2025, associated with the 34th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2025)
summary: General-purpose graphics processing unit (GPU) computing has emerged as a leading parallel computing paradigm, offering significant performance gains in various domains such as scientific computing and deep learning. However, GPU programs are susceptible to numerical bugs, which can lead to incorrect results or crashes. These bugs are difficult to detect, debug, and fix due to their dependence on specific input values or types and the absence of reliable error-checking mechanisms and oracles. Additionally, the unique programming conventions of GPUs complicate identifying the root causes of bugs, while fixing them requires domain-specific knowledge of GPU computing and numerical libraries. Therefore, understanding the characteristics of GPU numerical bugs (GPU-NBs) is crucial for developing effective solutions. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive study of GPU-NBs by analyzing 397 real-world bug samples from GitHub. We identify common root causes, symptoms, input patterns, test oracles that trigger these bugs and the strategies used to fix them. We also present GPU-NBDetect, a preliminary tool designed to detect numerical bugs across six distinct bug categories. GPU-NBDetect detected a total of 226 bugs across 186 mathematical functions in four libraries, with 60 of the bugs confirmed by developers. Our findings lay the groundwork for developing detection and prevention techniques for GPU-NBs and offer insights for building more effective debugging and auto-repair tool.

title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
summary: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

title: Towards Multi-Method Evaluation of AI in Health: Integrating Benchmarks, Autoraters, and Expert Evaluation
summary: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are being rapidly adopted in healthcare, but they are challenging to assess with traditional evaluation frameworks. These conceptual, methodological, and practical challenges parallel decades of work in evaluating clinician and health system quality and safety. We describe the adaptation of methods from several fields, combined with emerging technical approaches, into a structured, multi-method evaluation framework designed to give well-rounded assessments of GenAI in health at scale. The approach first anchors evaluation to Critical User Journeys (CUJs) to help prioritize out of a large choice space, and maps these to a phased AI system lifecycle (base model development, product development, and post-deployment monitoring), since evaluation at each stage requires different methodological approaches. In this context, the approach then integrates three distinct evaluation methods (closed-question benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge autoraters, and expert human review) across three core domains: accuracy, safety, and usefulness. Taken together, this approach provides a strategic framework for bridging the gap between benchmarking results and performance in the real world with the goal of supporting decision-making and accountability across development, procurement, and deployment for product teams, health systems, and regulators.

title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
summary: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io

title: High-fidelity training-free photovoltaic module mapping from multi-view UAV imagery
summary: High-fidelity photovoltaic (PV) module mapping requires complete instance recovery and accurate delineation. Vision foundation models offer zero-shot segmentation, but converting incomplete and inconsistent predictions across views into a complete, geometrically accurate map of individual modules remains challenging. We propose the Multi-View PV Module Mapper (MV-PVMapper), a training-free framework coupling vision foundation models with unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry. First, Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) generates candidates from original images using text prompts. Their contours are then transferred into object space through per-module slope correction to limit distortion from surface-model noise, and verified against representative module dimensions to guide cross-view instance selection. Finally, accepted instances return to all covering images as box prompts for SAM~3, supplementing text prompts with spatial cues for iterative segmentation, verification and fusion. On five-direction surveys of three operational rooftop PV plants at approximately 1 cm nadir ground sampling distance, two feedback iterations recover 7,710 of 7,711 reference modules with no false positives at an intersection-over-union (IoU) matching threshold of 0.5. Macro-averaged area precision and recall reach 99.00 % and 98.52 %, respectively. Averaged across sites, the aggregated Jaccard index reaches 97.55 %, compared with 60.73 % and 41.24 % for orthomosaic segmentation and multi-view pixel-voting baselines, respectively; average precision at the stricter IoU threshold of 0.95 reaches 95.67 %. Ablation studies show that module-size constraints are critical for instance separation, while slope correction and feedback to all covering views improve boundary accuracy. These results are achieved without task-specific image annotation or segmentation-model weight updates.

title: PAC Learning with Multiple Correct Answers
summary:
We study PAC learning when each example comes with a set of at most $\ell$ correct labels and a prediction is correct if it belongs to this set. Training may reveal the full set, only whether a proposed label is correct (bandit feedback), or one correct label chosen by a demonstrator (emonstrations).
  Our main finding is that demonstrations can be much harder than full sets, and even than bandit feedback, both in which classes can be learned and in how many examples are needed. For finite label spaces, a generalized Natarajan dimension characterizes learnability from full sets and from bandit feedback, in both the realizable and the agnostic setting. From demonstrations, however, a class is realizably learnable if and only if the intersections of at most $\ell+1$ of its hypotheses are learnable from full sets. Already with three labels, this condition can fail for a class learnable from a single full-set example or even a single bandit answer. When the condition holds, we show that $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-\ell})$ demonstrations suffice, and the exponent $\ell$ cannot be improved in general, even for classes learnable from $\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ full sets or bandit answers.
  For countable label spaces and $\ell \geq 2$, our packed dimension, which asks for many disjoint groups of at most $\ell+1$ hypotheses with no common label, characterizes full-set learnability, and demonstrations still reduce to intersections. Agnostic learning from demonstrations, already for finite label spaces, is not determined by the dimensions of the intersection class that characterize realizable learning.
  Finally, we show that the uniform bound $\ell$ on the number of correct labels is essential. Without this bound, it is impossible to characterize learnability by any dimension determined by finite subclasses.

title: Sharp Bounds for Truthful-in-Expectation Scheduling
summary: We study randomized mechanisms for scheduling indivisible jobs on $n$ unrelated machines. Each machine is controlled by a selfish agent who privately knows its processing time for each job. A mechanism assigns every job to a machine and makes payments. We require truthfulness in expectation: no agent can increase its expected payment minus its expected processing cost by misreporting, regardless of the other agents' reports. The makespan is the maximum total processing time assigned to a machine; the objective is to minimize its expectation. We prove that the optimal approximation ratio is $(n+1)/2$ for every $n\ge7$, relative to the minimum makespan of an integral assignment. The lower bound holds for every $n$ and allows unrestricted computation and arbitrary correlations among assignments, assuming finite expected payments and a guarantee uniform over all finite job counts. The matching mechanism uses correlated rounding and runs in expected polynomial bit time on rational inputs. These guarantees hold for all finite nonnegative processing times. For two machines, we characterize the optimal approximation ratio exactly as an analytic constant, approximately $1.505995705434$, and give a mechanism attaining it. For three machines the optimal ratio is $2$. For four, five, and six machines we obtain upper bounds of $3$, $105/32$, and $29/8$, respectively, compared with the general lower bound $(n+1)/2$. The proofs for $n\ge7$ do not rely on computer-assisted certificates; the two- and three-machine results use exact rational computer-assisted certificates.

title: From Opinions to Commitments: Unstable Assignments and Silent Choices in AI-Mediated Proposals
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to turn citizens' opinions into collective proposals.
